definition.text: HTTP is a stateless, application-layer request-response protocol that clients and servers use to exchange hypertext and other content, and it is the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web.

facts.text: HTTP is a request-response protocol in the client-server model: a client sends a request, and the server returns a response that describes the outcome and may carry a resource such as an HTML document.
A web browser is the usual client and a web server the usual server; other user agents include web crawlers, voice browsers and mobile apps.
HTTP is stateless: the server is not required to retain information about each user across multiple requests.
HTTP needs a reliable transport underneath; before HTTP/3 the standard choice is TCP, typically on port 80 when unencrypted and port 443 when encrypted.
A web resource is located by a URL, using the http and https URI schemes.
HTTP lets intermediaries such as web caches and proxy servers improve or enable communication; browsers also cache resources they have fetched to reduce network traffic.
Some headers are managed hop by hop by intermediaries, while others are managed end to end, only by the source client and the target web server.

RFC 9110 defines the overall architecture, common terminology and the semantics shared by all versions of HTTP; the semantics are not versioned, so methods, status codes and fields mean the same in every version.

definition.text: An HTTP message is a header followed by an optional body; clients send request messages and servers answer with response messages.

facts.text: A request's start line holds the method name, the request URI and the protocol version, such as GET /customer/123 HTTP/1.1.
A response's start line holds the protocol version, a status code and optionally a reason phrase, such as HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request.
Header fields are name-value pairs separated by a colon that carry metadata about the message; software uses them more than users see them.
A header field name is matched ignoring case, unlike a method name, which must match exactly.
In HTTP/1.1 every request header field except Host is optional.
The body may hold data in any format, which must match the Content-Type header field when the message has one, and a body can be blank.
The standards do not limit header size or count, but most servers, clients and proxies impose limits for practical and security reasons.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 messages are binary, compress headers with HPACK or QPACK, and replace the request or response line with pseudo-header fields.

title: HTTP request methods

definition.text: The request method, informally a verb, is the primary source of request semantics: it names the action the client wants applied to the target resource.

facts.text: GET retrieves a current representation of a resource and should only read data; it is the primary retrieval mechanism and the focus of almost all performance optimizations, and its URL can be bookmarked, shared and cached.

HEAD is identical to GET except that the server must not send content, so a client can obtain the headers, such as Content-Length, or test links and recent modifications without transferring the representation.

POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation by its own semantics, such as submitting form data, posting a message or creating a resource, which is reported with 201 (Created) and a Location header.
PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state with the state in the request; unlike POST the client chooses the target URI, and repeating the same PUT updates the same resource.

DELETE asks the origin server to remove the association between a resource and its current functionality, like rm in UNIX; PATCH applies a partial modification, saving bandwidth compared with a full PUT.

CONNECT asks a proxy to open a tunnel to the destination server, commonly so TLS can run through it; OPTIONS asks for a resource's communication options; TRACE loops the request message back for testing and diagnostics.
General-purpose servers must support GET and HEAD, and all other methods are optional; an unrecognized method should get 501 (Not Implemented) and a known but disallowed one 405 (Method Not Allowed).

Responses to GET and HEAD are cacheable and POST only with explicit freshness information and a matching Content-Location; responses to PUT and DELETE are not cacheable, and a successful one invalidates stored responses for that URI.

notes: Sources: Wikipedia HTTP (Method), ByteByteGo top-9 guide, RFC 9110 section 9. Wikipedia says POST responses are cacheable; RFC 9110 qualifies this (explicit freshness plus Content-Location), so the RFC's wording is used. PATCH is defined outside RFC 9110 (RFC 5789 per Wikipedia).

title: Safe HTTP methods
article: HTTP#Message format > Request > Method > Safe method

definition.text: A request method is safe if its defined semantics are essentially read-only: the client does not request or expect any state change on the origin server.

facts.text: RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as safe, the later QUERY method is also safe, and POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT and PATCH are not.
Distinguishing safe from unsafe methods lets automated retrieval by spiders and cache prefetching work without fear of causing harm, and lets a user agent warn the user before an unsafe action.
Reasonable use of a safe method is not expected to cause harm, loss of property or unusual burden on the server.
A safe method may still have side effects the client did not request and cannot be blamed for, such as appending to an access log or charging an advertising account.
A resource cannot treat a request inconsistently with its method's semantics: even if the URI suggests an unsafe action, a client can expect it to avoid unsafe actions for a safe method.

When URI parameters select an action, such as page?do=delete, the resource owner must disable the unsafe action for safe methods, or automated GETs for link maintenance, prefetching or indexing will cause side effects.

Nothing technically stops a server from changing state on a GET, but this is discouraged because caches, search engines and other automated agents may then make unintended changes, as with a delete URL fetched by GET.

title: Idempotent HTTP methods
article: HTTP#Message format > Request > Method > Idempotent method

definition.text: A request method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of several identical requests with it is the same as the effect of a single such request.

facts.text: PUT, DELETE and all safe methods are idempotent; POST, CONNECT and PATCH are not necessarily, so an identical POST sent twice may modify state again or send two emails.

Identical GET, PUT or DELETE requests give the same outcome as one request: a PUT that sets an email to the value already recorded changes nothing, and deleting an already deleted user has no further effect.
Idempotency covers only what the client requested: a server may still log each request or keep revision history for each idempotent request.

Idempotent requests can be repeated automatically if a communication failure happens before the client reads the response: after a PUT whose connection closed, the client can reconnect and retry, knowing the effect is the same.

A client should not automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless it knows the request is really idempotent or can detect the original was never applied; a proxy must never do so, and a failed retry should not be retried.
Some clients take a riskier approach and retry a POST when the connection closed before any part of a response arrived, particularly on an idle persistent connection.
Duplicate POSTs can happen by accident, for example a user clicking a button again without feedback, so it is generally up to the web application to keep a POST from being processed twice.

Neither the protocol nor the web server enforces idempotency; an application can trigger a database insert from a GET, which goes against recommendations and risks harm if a user agent assumes repeating the request is safe.

definition.text: An HTTP status code is a three-digit number in a response that describes the result of the request and the semantics of the response.

facts.text: Valid codes run from 100 to 599; the first digit gives the class and the last two digits have no categorization role: informational (100-199), success (200-299), redirection (300-399), client error (400-499) and server error (500-599).

1xx means the request was received and processing continues, 2xx that it was accepted, 3xx that more action is needed, 4xx that it is malformed or cannot be fulfilled, and 5xx that the server failed on a valid-looking request.

A client may not know every status code, but it must understand the class from the first digit and treat an unrecognized code as the x00 code of that class; an unrecognized 471 is treated like 400 (Bad Request).
A client that receives an invalid status code should treat the response as a 5xx.
A single request can have zero or more interim 1xx responses followed by exactly one final response.
A client handles a response mainly by its status code and secondarily by its header fields; the response usually carries a representation that explains the status.
Status codes are extensible and registered in the HTTP Status Code Registry; the reason phrase after the code is only a recommendation and human-readable, while the code is machine-readable.

Responses with heuristically cacheable codes, such as 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414 and 501, can be reused by a cache with heuristic expiration unless the method or cache controls say otherwise.

definition.text: A persistent connection lets one TCP connection be reused for more than one HTTP request and response.

facts.text: HTTP/0.9 always closed the TCP connection after the response and HTTP/1.0 should do so, so each resource needed a new connection; HTTP/1.1 officially introduced keep-alive so a connection could be reused.
Persistent connections cut latency because the client does not repeat the TCP 3-way handshake, and the connection tends to speed up over time because of TCP's slow-start mechanism.
HTTP pipelining added in HTTP/1.1 lets a client send several requests before waiting for each response.

Pipelining was never really safe because some servers and many proxies mishandled it, serving only the first request, closing the connection or returning responses out of order; it was disabled and then removed from most browsers.
HTTP/2 extends persistent connections by multiplexing many concurrent requests and responses through a single TCP/IP connection, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP instead of TCP.
Either the client or the server can close a connection at any time, usually announced by HTTP headers in the last request or response.

title: HTTP versions

definition.text: HTTP has evolved through versions 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3, each changing how requests share connections and which transport carries them.

facts.text: HTTP/0.9 (1991) and HTTP/1.0 (1996) are obsolete, while HTTP/1.1 (1997), HTTP/2 (2015) and HTTP/3 (2022) are standard.
HTTP/1 and its sub-versions introduced persistent connections, pipelining and headers, built on top of TCP; HTTP/1.0 used a separate TCP connection per resource request, while HTTP/1.1 reuses one.
HTTP/2 brought multiplexing, stream prioritization, server push and HPACK compression, but still ran over TCP.
HTTP/2 sends compressed binary headers, uses one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8, and splits traffic into bidirectional streams that almost solve head-of-line blocking.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which is built on UDP, so it moves away from TCP.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do not obsolete the earlier major versions.

conflicts.note: The guide dates HTTP/3 to 2019; Wikipedia's version table gives 2022 for the standard (RFC 9114 on 6 June 2022) and says support was first added in 2019. Not the same event, so the table value is stated.

title: HTTP/2

definition.text: HTTP/2 is a revision of HTTP that maps HTTP semantics onto binary frames multiplexed over one connection, for lower latency and more efficient use of the network than HTTP/1.1.

facts.text: HTTP/2 supports all core HTTP features but uses network resources more efficiently and cuts latency by compressing HTTP fields and allowing multiple concurrent exchanges on the same connection.

HTTP/1.0 allowed one outstanding request per TCP connection and HTTP/1.1 pipelining only partly helped, so clients opened several connections; HTTP/2 needs one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8.

Messages are encoded in binary and split into frames, which makes processing more efficient; each request and response exchange gets its own stream, and frames of many streams are interleaved and reassembled on the other side.
HTTP fields are repetitive and verbose, so HTTP/2 compresses them with HPACK, saving bandwidth and allowing many requests to be compressed into one packet.

Prioritization matters for performance, but the RFC 7540 priority signaling proved complex and unevenly implemented, so RFC 9113 deprecates it and encourages an alternative scheme such as HTTP-PRIORITY.

Server push, an optional mode, lets a server speculatively send data the client will probably need, trading network usage for latency, but it is difficult to use effectively because the server must predict the client's requests.
Over TLS, HTTP/2 is negotiated with the ALPN extension under the identifier h2, and implementations MUST use TLS 1.2 or higher.
HTTP/2 does not address TCP head-of-line blocking, and it can still be slow in some scenarios, so developers need to test and optimize to get its benefits.

conflicts.text: With stream prioritization, developers can customize the relative weight of requests or streams so the server sends more frames for higher-priority requests.
conflicts.note: Older curated description; RFC 9113 (standard tier) deprecates the RFC 7540 priority signaling, so the standard's version is stated.

notes: Replaces the ByteByteGo-based entry; keeps its binary framing, multiplexing, HPACK and TLS facts, and corrects prioritization to RFC 9113.

title: HTTP/3 and QUIC

definition.text: HTTP/3 is the third major version of HTTP, which runs over QUIC, a multiplexed transport built on UDP, instead of over TCP.

facts.text: HTTP/3 is specified in RFC 9114 and uses QUIC (RFC 9000), a multiplexed transport built on UDP that provides reliability and does congestion control in user space, so HTTP has moved away from TCP.
HTTP/3 keeps the semantics of earlier versions, with the same request methods, status codes and message fields; the differences lie in how they are encoded and mapped to the underlying transport.

QUIC fixes HTTP/2's head-of-line blocking: TCP cannot see HTTP/2's parallel streams, so one lost packet stalls every transaction, while QUIC's native multiplexing makes a lost packet affect only the streams that lost data.

HTTP/3 compresses headers with QPACK instead of HPACK; QPACK sends table updates on separate unidirectional streams to reduce compression-related head-of-line blocking among independently delivered QUIC streams.
The HTTPS DNS resource record (RFC 9460) lets a client connect without first receiving an Alt-Svc header from an earlier HTTP version, removing the 1 RTT of TCP handshaking.
HTTP/3 has lower latency and loads faster than earlier versions in real-world use, in some cases over four times faster than HTTP/1.1, which for many websites is the only HTTP version deployed.
As of July 2026, more than 95% of major web browsers in use and 40% of the top 10 million websites support HTTP/3.

conflicts.text: HTTP/3 has lower latency and loads faster than HTTP/2, in some cases over three times faster than HTTP/1.1.

definition.text: HTTP is stateless, so the meaning of each request can be understood in isolation, and a web application that must remember a user across requests builds its own session on top.

facts.text: As a stateless protocol, HTTP does not require the web server to retain information or status about each user across multiple requests; each request's semantics can be understood in isolation, whatever connection it arrives on.
Many implementations depend on this stateless design to reuse proxied connections or to dynamically load balance requests across multiple servers.
A server must not assume two requests on the same connection come from the same user agent unless the connection is secured and specific to that agent.
A web application that needs a session implements it with HTTP cookies, hidden variables in a web form or another mechanism.
A session typically starts with an interactive login and ends with a logout, using a custom authentication mechanism rather than HTTP authentication.

definition.text: HTTP provides a general framework for access control, with extensible challenge-response schemes the server uses to challenge a request and the client uses to supply credentials.

facts.text: Schemes such as basic and digest authentication work by challenge and response: the server issues a challenge before serving the requested content; new schemes are registered in the HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry.

An origin server challenges a request with 401 (Unauthorized) and must include a WWW-Authenticate header listing at least one challenge; the client answers with an Authorization header carrying its credentials.
Valid credentials that are not adequate to gain access should get 403 (Forbidden), not 401.

A protection space is the server's origin combined with the realm value, so realms partition a server's resources into spaces with their own scheme or authorization database; credentials can be reused across one space.

title: What happens when you type a URL

definition.text: When a URL is entered, the browser resolves the domain to an IP address, opens a TCP connection, sends an HTTP request and renders the server's response.

facts.text: The URL has a scheme (http://, telling the browser to connect using HTTP), a domain (the site's domain name) and a path on the server to the requested resource.
The browser looks up the domain's IP address with a DNS lookup, which is sped up by caches at the browser, OS, local network and ISP.
If no cache has the address, the browser goes to DNS servers for a recursive DNS lookup until the IP address is found.
With the IP address, the browser establishes a TCP connection and sends an HTTP request such as GET /phone HTTP/1.1 with a Host header.
The server processes the request and sends back a response, with status code 200 for success, and the browser renders the HTML content.

title: Symmetric session keys in HTTPS
article: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/how-does-https-work.md#Why does HTTPS switch to symmetric encryption during data transmission?

definition.text: HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption only to set up a session key and then switches to symmetric encryption for the data.

facts.text: Once client and server hold the same session key, the encrypted data travels over a secure bi-directional channel using symmetric encryption.
Asymmetric encryption works only one way, so data the server encrypted for the client could be decrypted by anyone holding the public key.
Asymmetric encryption adds a lot of mathematical overhead for the server, so it is not suitable for data transmission in long sessions.

definition.text: SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, is a protocol for encrypting and securing communications on the internet, now deprecated in favor of TLS.

facts.text: SSL was first developed in 1995 and has since been deprecated in favor of TLS, yet most major certificate providers still call certificates SSL certificates.
Web data was originally sent in plaintext that anyone who intercepted it could read, and SSL was created to fix this and protect user privacy.
By encrypting data between the user and a web server, SSL also stops certain attacks by preventing tampering with data in transit.

definition.text: Mutual TLS, or mTLS, is a method of mutual authentication in which both ends of a connection verify that the other holds the correct private key.

facts.text: TLS can run in a simple mode, where only the server authenticates, or a mutual mode, which requires the user to install a personal client certificate in the browser.
In a client-authenticated handshake the server requests a certificate, and the client sends its certificate plus a signature made with its private key, which proves it owns the certificate.
mTLS keeps traffic secure and trusted in both directions between client and server, adding a layer of security for users logging in to an organization's network or applications.
Microservices and distributed systems commonly use mTLS to verify each other in a zero trust security model.

definition.text: HTTPS is HTTP carried over an encrypted TLS connection, so web traffic is private, authenticated and protected from tampering in transit.

facts.text: The main motivations for HTTPS are authentication of the accessed website and protection of the privacy and integrity of exchanged data in transit.
HTTPS is not a separate protocol but ordinary HTTP over an encrypted SSL/TLS connection; its URLs begin with https:// and use port 443 by default, while HTTP uses port 80.

Plain HTTP is not encrypted, so it is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle and eavesdropping attacks that expose accounts and sensitive information or inject malware and advertisements into pages; HTTPS is designed to withstand them.
Because HTTP runs entirely on top of TLS, the URL, query parameters, headers, cookies and message data can all be encrypted.
Usually only the server is authenticated, by the client examining its certificate, which a trusted third party must sign; TLS still protects the channel when only one side is authenticated.
TLS typically uses long-term public and private keys to generate a short-term session key that encrypts the data flow between client and server; a hijacker of the traffic gets only binary data.
For HTTPS to be effective a whole site must be served over it: loading scripts or images over HTTP, or only a login page over HTTPS, leaves users open to attacks and surveillance.
Deploying HTTPS also allows HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, which are designed to reduce page load times, size and latency.

title: Transport Layer Security

definition.text: TLS is a cryptographic protocol that provides secured communications over a computer network, giving applications privacy, integrity and authenticity.

facts.text: TLS does three things: encryption hides the data from third parties, authentication ensures the parties are who they claim to be, and integrity verifies the data has not been forged or tampered with.
TLS is used in email, instant messaging and voice over IP, but securing HTTPS is its most visible use; a primary use is encrypting communication between web applications and servers.
TLS evolved from SSL and is an IETF standard first defined in 1999; the current version is TLS 1.3, defined in August 2018.
TLS is made of two layers, the record protocol and the handshake protocol, and runs on top of a reliable transport such as TCP.

Because applications can run with or without TLS, the client must ask the server for a TLS connection, either with a separate port (443 for HTTPS rather than 80 for HTTP) or with a protocol-specific STARTTLS request.
The handshake uses an asymmetric cipher to set the cipher parameters and a session-specific shared key, and further communication is encrypted with a symmetric cipher.

A TLS connection is private because a symmetric key, unique to each connection and negotiated at the start, encrypts the data; it is authenticated with public-key cryptography, required for the server and optional for the client.
Each message carries a message authentication code, so lost or altered data is detected.

notes: Singh says this topic is 'not very important' for big-picture system design but good to know (b2ffffd6e312).

title: TLS handshake
article: Transport Layer Security#Protocol details > TLS handshake

definition.text: In the TLS handshake the client and server agree on cipher parameters, the server proves its identity with a certificate, and both derive a shared session key for the secured connection.

facts.text: The client sends a ClientHello with the highest TLS version it supports, a random number, and its suggested cipher suites and compression methods; the server answers with a ServerHello choosing from them, ideally the highest version both support.

The server usually sends a digital certificate holding its name, the trusted certificate authority that vouches for it, and its public key; the client confirms the certificate is valid before proceeding.
In older TLS and SSL the client encrypts a random PreMasterSecret with the server's public key and the server decrypts it with its private key; both then derive the session key from it.

Alternatively Diffie-Hellman key exchange, or its elliptic-curve variant, generates the session key with forward secrecy; TLS 1.3 eliminated the PreMasterSecret approach when it mandated forward secrecy.
Both sides compute a master secret from the random numbers and key material, and all other key data for the connection, such as the encryption key and MAC key, is derived from it.

Each side then sends a Finished message, authenticated and encrypted, containing a hash and MAC over the previous handshake messages, and the other side verifies it; if any verification fails, the handshake fails and no connection is created.
Once the handshake completes, both sides hold the same session key and data flows over a secure bi-directional channel, encrypted and decrypted with that key until the connection closes.
The TLS 1.3 handshake takes one round trip instead of the two earlier versions need, because the client guesses the key exchange algorithm and sends public keys for its guesses in the ClientHello.

notes: Merges the ByteByteGo how-does-https-work steps (RSA-style key transport) with Wikipedia's account; Wikipedia says that key-transport form was eliminated in TLS 1.3, so the entry says it applies to older versions.

title: TLS session resumption
article: rfc>8446#2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Resumption and Pre-Shared Key (PSK)

definition.text: A resumed TLS session reuses the results of an earlier handshake, through a session ID, a session ticket or, in TLS 1.3, a pre-shared key, so the handshake can skip expensive public-key operations.

facts.text: Public key operations such as RSA are relatively expensive in computational power, and resumed sessions give a secure shortcut around them.

With session IDs the server maps the ID to the previously negotiated master secret and the client sends the ID on reconnecting; both sides must hold the same master secret or the resumed handshake fails.
With session tickets the server stores its session state in an encrypted and authenticated ticket that the client keeps and presents later, so the server stores no per-session state.
Session tickets can undermine forward secrecy, because long-lived ticket keys defeat the protection of forward secrecy cipher suites.

TLS 1.3 replaces session IDs and tickets with one PSK exchange: the server sends a ticket after the handshake, the client offers it in a later ClientHello, and if accepted its key bootstraps the new connection without a full handshake.

A PSK combined with (EC)DHE keeps forward secrecy, while a PSK alone loses it for application data; the client SHOULD also send a key_share so the server can decline and fall back to a full handshake.

A ticket is an opaque label, either a database lookup key or a self-encrypted, self-authenticated value; servers MUST NOT set a lifetime above 604800 seconds (7 days), and clients MUST NOT cache a ticket longer than 7 days.

Servers may send several tickets on one connection, useful for opening multiple parallel HTTP connections; a resumed handshake omits Certificate and CertificateVerify because the server authenticates with the PSK.

title: Forward secrecy

definition.text: Forward secrecy is a property of a cryptographic system that keeps a session key safe even if one of the private keys is compromised in the future.

facts.text: Without forward secrecy, a compromised server private key exposes all future sessions that use its certificate and also any past sessions that were intercepted and stored.
TLS can provide it by requiring ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish session keys; only the DHE and ECDHE exchanges provide forward secrecy.
Having one of the long-term asymmetric keys used to establish an HTTPS session should not make it easier to derive the short-term session key and decrypt the conversation later.
TLS 1.3 mandates forward secrecy by using ephemeral keys in the key agreement and drops support for ciphers and key exchanges without it, such as static RSA.
Many clients and servers are not configured to require it, so without Diffie-Hellman a third party that obtains the server's private key can decrypt all recorded traffic.
Session tickets and weak Diffie-Hellman parameters can weaken the forward secrecy a server tries to provide.

definition.text: A digital certificate certifies that a named subject owns a public key, and certificate authorities are trusted third parties that sign certificates so others can rely on them.

facts.text: A certificate lets relying parties trust signatures and assertions made by the private key that matches the certified public key.
A TLS server certificate holds the server name, the trusted certificate authority that vouches for it, and the server's public key.
TLS typically relies on trusted third-party certificate authorities, and trust is anchored in a list of certificates shipped with user agent software such as the browser.
X.509 certificates make a certificate authority and public key infrastructure necessary to verify the link between a certificate and its owner and to generate, sign and administer certificates.
To serve HTTPS, an administrator creates a certificate for the web server and has a trusted certificate authority sign it, otherwise browsers warn users.
Commercial certificate authorities sell certificates, and a free automated service such as Let's Encrypt issues basic ones.
Certificate authorities are a security weak point: if one cooperates or is compromised, man-in-the-middle attacks become possible.

title: Certificate revocation
article: HTTPS#Technical > Server setup > In case of compromised secret (private) key > Certificate revocation

definition.text: A certificate can be revoked before it expires, for example because its private key was compromised, and browsers check whether that has happened.

facts.text: With the Online Certificate Status Protocol, the browser sends the certificate's serial number to the certificate authority, which answers whether the certificate is still valid.
The authority may also publish a certificate revocation list naming revoked certificates; the CA/Browser forum no longer requires CRLs, but they are still widely used.
TLS 1.3 adds support for sending multiple OCSP responses.
Revocation is performed by the issuing CA with a cryptographically authenticated statement; without it, an attacker could exploit a compromised or misissued certificate until it expires.

notes: more on the existing entry: adds the revocation trade-offs and fail-hard versus fail-soft choice; only the new facts.

title: TLS versions

definition.text: TLS has gone through versions 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, each defined in an RFC and each revised to address security threats.

facts.text: TLS 1.1 was defined in RFC 4346 in April 2006, TLS 1.2 in RFC 5246 in August 2008, and TLS 1.3 in RFC 8446 in August 2018.
TLS 1.3 supports 1-RTT handshakes with initial 0-RTT support and mandates perfect forward secrecy through ephemeral keys in the (EC)DH key agreement.
TLS 1.3 drops insecure or obsolete features, including compression, renegotiation, non-AEAD ciphers and static RSA and static DH key exchanges, and it prohibits SSL or RC4 negotiation.
TLS 1.3 encrypts all handshake messages after the ServerHello, including the server certificate.

notes: TLS 1.3 sentence 252da17ee0b9 also says 'updated with RFC 9846 in July 2026'; not used. Browser-support sentence is dated (March 2025).

title: TLS cipher suites and key exchange
article: Transport Layer Security#Algorithms > Key exchange or key agreement

definition.text: Before sending protected data, a TLS client and server must agree on an encryption key and a cipher, choosing among several key exchange, cipher and integrity methods.

facts.text: The client presents the cipher suites (ciphers and hash functions) it supports and the server picks one it also supports and tells the client.
Key exchange or agreement methods include RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, their elliptic-curve variants, anonymous Diffie-Hellman, pre-shared key and Secure Remote Password.

Anonymous Diffie-Hellman does not authenticate the server or user and is rarely used because it is open to man-in-the-middle attacks, and only the ephemeral DHE and ECDHE methods provide forward secrecy.
A message authentication code protects data integrity: HMAC is used for CBC mode block ciphers, while authenticated encryption such as GCM and CCM has an integrated MAC.

title: Server Name Indication
article: Transport Layer Security#Support for name-based virtual servers

definition.text: Server Name Indication is a TLS extension in which the client names the host it wants in its ClientHello, so a server hosting several sites can send the right certificate.

facts.text: The TLS handshake happens before the application protocol starts, so the server must choose a certificate right after the ClientHello and co-hosted name-based virtual servers would share one certificate.
This forces a hosting provider to share one certificate among customers or give each customer its own IP address.

Two X.509 workarounds exist: a wildcard certificate when all virtual servers share a domain, or listing every virtual host name in the subjectAltName extension, which needs reissuing whenever a server is added.
SNI sends the host name before the connection is encrypted, although older browsers do not support it.

definition.text: HTTPS protects content in transit but leaves some information visible and depends on correct implementation and on clients actually using it.

facts.text: Website addresses and port numbers are part of the underlying TCP/IP protocols, so an eavesdropper can still see the server's IP address and port, sometimes the domain name, and the amount and duration of traffic.
Traffic analysis can infer properties of encrypted traffic because TLS changes the contents but has minimal impact on the size and timing of traffic.
SSL stripping turns an https link into an http link so the attacker talks in clear with the client; HTTP Strict Transport Security is the countermeasure and is recommended alongside HTTPS.
The level of protection depends on correct implementation of the software and the cryptographic algorithms in use.

definition.text: TLS interception is decrypting, reading and re-encrypting an encrypted data stream in transit, usually through a transparent proxy.

facts.text: The interception software terminates the incoming TLS connection, inspects the HTTP plaintext, and opens a new TLS connection to the destination.
Network operators use it to scan for malware that encryption would otherwise hide.

It creates risks of its own: traffic is unencrypted at the interception point, which attracts attackers, and the operator or anyone who gains access to the system can mount man-in-the-middle attacks on users.

title: Datagram Transport Layer Security
article: Transport Layer Security#Description > Datagram Transport Layer Security

definition.text: Datagram TLS (DTLS) is a protocol based on TLS that secures datagram-based applications against eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery.

facts.text: DTLS is intended to give security guarantees similar to TLS but works with datagram protocols such as UDP, not only stream protocols.

Because it preserves the semantics of the underlying transport, an application avoids the delays of stream protocols but must handle packet reordering, datagram loss and data larger than one datagram.
Using UDP or SCTP rather than TCP avoids the TCP meltdown problem when creating a VPN tunnel.
All modern web browsers support DTLS-SRTP for WebRTC.

title: HTTP resources and representations
article: rfc>9110#3. Terminology and Core Concepts > 3.2. Representations

definition.text: A resource is the target of an HTTP request, and a representation is information reflecting the past, current or desired state of a resource in a format the protocol can carry.

facts.text: HTTP gives clients a uniform interface to a resource, whatever its type or implementation, by sending messages that manipulate or transfer representations.
HTTP does not limit what a resource is; most are identified by a URI, and request semantics live in the request method rather than in the identifier.

Because HTTP communicates a transferable representation instead of the resource itself, implementation details stay hidden and a resource can be anything, even a temporal function such as the current weather.

A resource can have several representations; an algorithm, usually content negotiation, picks the selected representation, which supplies data and metadata for conditional requests and for 200, 206 and 304 responses to GET.

title: HTTP intermediaries
article: rfc>9110#3. Terminology and Core Concepts > 3.7. Intermediaries

definition.text: An HTTP intermediary is a proxy, gateway or tunnel placed between client and origin server so a request can be satisfied through a chain of connections.

facts.text: A message that travels a chain with three intermediaries passes through four separate connections, and an option may apply to the nearest neighbor, only the endpoints, or every connection.
A proxy is chosen by the client, usually through local configuration, to receive requests for some absolute URIs; organizations use proxies for security services, annotation or shared caching.

A gateway, also called a reverse proxy, acts as the origin server toward the client but translates requests and forwards them inbound; it serves legacy services, accelerator caching and load balancing across machines.
A tunnel is a blind relay between two connections that does not change messages, for example carrying TLS through a firewall proxy, and it ends when both ends close.
An interception proxy, or transparent proxy, is not chosen by the client but filters or redirects outgoing port 80 traffic; at the protocol level it is indistinguishable from an on-path attacker.
Each proxy must append a Via header describing how it received the message, which helps track forwards and avoid request loops.
Intermediaries are inherently placed for on-path attacks, and one that holds a shared cache is especially vulnerable to cache poisoning.

definition.text: POST hands the enclosed representation to the resource to process by its own semantics, while PUT replaces the target resource's state with it.

facts.text: The fundamental difference is the intent for the enclosed representation: the target of a POST handles it by the resource's own semantics, whereas a PUT replaces the state of the target resource.
Hence the intent of PUT is idempotent and visible to intermediaries, though only the origin server knows the exact effect.
A proper PUT presumes the client knows which resource it wants; a service that selects the URI itself after receiving a state-changing request should use POST instead.

A successful PUT returns 201 (Created) if it created the resource and 200 (OK) or 204 (No Content) if it modified an existing one, while a POST that creates resources should return 201 with a Location header.

title: HTTP content negotiation

definition.text: Content negotiation is how HTTP chooses among several representations of a resource, such as different formats, languages or encodings, to fit what a client can handle or prefers.

facts.text: HTTP defines proactive negotiation, where the server picks from the client's stated preferences, reactive negotiation, where the server lists options for the client to choose, and request content negotiation, where the client uses the server's stated preferences.

In proactive negotiation the client sends preferences in Accept, Accept-Charset, Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language headers, and the server also weighs implicit hints such as the client's network address or User-Agent.
Proactive negotiation helps when the selection algorithm is hard to describe to the client or the server wants to send its best guess with the first response, saving a round trip.

Its disadvantages: the server cannot know what is best for each user, describing capabilities in every request is inefficient and a privacy risk, it complicates the server, and it limits reuse of responses by shared caches.

In reactive negotiation the client selects after an initial response, often from a list of alternatives such as in 300 (Multiple Choices) and 406 (Not Acceptable) responses, by requesting one of them.

Reactive negotiation suits responses that vary on common dimensions, servers that cannot learn client capabilities, and public caches that spread load, but it costs a second request and list-sending latency.
A q parameter gives each preference a weight from 0 to 1, where 1 is most preferred, 0.001 least and 0 means not acceptable; the default weight is 1.
A client cannot rely on proactive preferences being honored, since the server may send a non-conforming response instead of 406; the Vary header tells which request information the server used.

related: HTTP content type, encoding and length

title: Vary header
article: rfc>9110#12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary

definition.text: The Vary response header names the request fields, beyond method and URI, that may have influenced which content the origin server chose.

facts.text: Its value is a list of selecting header field names, such as accept-encoding and accept-language, or the wildcard *.
For caches, a response with Vary may be reused only for a later request with the same values in the listed fields, unless the origin validates it, so Vary expands the cache key.

An origin server should send Vary on a cacheable response it wants selectively reused, for example when it chose the language from Accept-Language, but may omit it when the variance matters less than the caching cost.
A * signals that other aspects of the request, even outside the message, such as the client's network address, played a role, so a cache cannot judge reuse without asking the origin.

title: HTTP content type, encoding and length
article: rfc>9110#8. Representation Data and Metadata > 8.4. Content-Encoding

definition.text: Representation metadata describes the content of a message: Content-Type gives its media type, Content-Encoding the codings applied, such as compression, and Content-Length its size in octets.

facts.text: The media type in Content-Type defines both the data format and how the recipient should process it after any content codings are decoded; a sender should include it unless the type is unknown.
Content-Encoding lists the content codings applied beyond the media type, mainly so data can be compressed without losing its media type, for example gzip.
Accept-Encoding states which content codings a client accepts, the acceptable coding with the highest non-zero weight is preferred, and identity means no encoding.

When the length is unknown in advance, Content-Length is omitted and a client taking a close as the end cannot tell a premature close from a complete response; chunked transfer encoding streams content reliably instead.

definition.text: A conditional request carries header fields that set a precondition to be tested before the method is applied to the target resource.

facts.text: Conditional GET is the most efficient mechanism for HTTP cache updates, and conditionals on state-changing methods such as PUT and DELETE prevent the lost update problem, where one client overwrites another's work.
Each precondition compares validators from earlier representations with the current validators, so it tests whether the resource changed since a state the client knows.
HTTP/1.0 added headers for conditional GET: the server returns the full content only if the client does not know the last modified time or it changed since the last full response.

If-None-Match is mainly used in conditional GET to update caches cheaply; if a listed tag matches, the server answers 304 (Not Modified) for GET and HEAD and 412 (Precondition Failed) for other methods.
If-Modified-Since makes a GET or HEAD conditional on a newer modification date, and it is ignored when If-None-Match is present; caches build it from the cached Last-Modified value.
If-Match makes a method conditional on the current entity tag matching, using strong comparison; it is mostly used with POST, PUT and DELETE to prevent lost updates, and a failure gets 412.
If-None-Match with * stops an unsafe method such as PUT from overwriting a representation when the client believes none exists, a variant of the lost update problem.
When several preconditions are present they are evaluated in order: If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, then If-Range.

title: HTTP validators and entity tags
article: rfc>9110#8. Representation Data and Metadata > 8.8. Validator Fields

definition.text: A validator is resource metadata that can be used in a precondition to make a conditional request; HTTP defines modification dates and opaque entity tags.

facts.text: An ETag is an opaque quoted string that identifies one representation of a resource, whether the versions differ over time or through content negotiation.
An entity tag can be more reliable than a modification date when storing dates is inconvenient, one-second resolution is not enough, or dates are not consistently maintained.

A strong validator changes whenever the observable representation data changes and is unique across all versions of a resource's representations over time; weak validators, marked W/, are easy to generate but less useful for comparison.
In a successful response to a state-changing request, a validator such as the ETag in a 201 describes the new representation, so later conditional requests can prevent lost updates.

definition.text: A range request asks for only part of a representation, such as the remainder of an interrupted download, by sending a Range header on a GET.

facts.text: Range requests help when transfers are interrupted by canceled requests or dropped connections, and when devices with limited storage want only a subset, such as one page of a large document.
A server fulfilling a range request sends 206 (Partial Content); a single part needs a Content-Range header, and several parts are sent as multipart/byteranges.
A server answers 416 (Range Not Satisfiable) when no requested range is satisfiable or the client asks for an excessive number of small or overlapping ranges, a potential denial of service attack.
Accept-Ranges: bytes advertises support and Accept-Ranges: none says it is unsupported; a client may try ranges regardless and must not assume a later range request will return a partial response.

definition.text: The 2xx class says the client's request was successfully received, understood and accepted.

facts.text: 200 (OK) means the request succeeded, and the content sent depends on the request method.
201 (Created) means one or more new resources were created; the primary one is identified by the Location header or, if absent, by the target URI.
202 (Accepted) means the request was accepted for processing but not completed, and it may never be acted on; HTTP has no way to send the final status of an asynchronous operation later.
204 (No Content) means the request succeeded with nothing more to send, and 206 (Partial Content) means a range request is being fulfilled.

definition.text: The 3xx class says the user agent must take further action to fulfill the request, usually by repeating it at a different URI.

facts.text: Redirects point to another URI in the Location header (301, 302, 307, 308), offer a choice of representations (300), send the client to a different resource (303), or point to a stored result (304).

301 (Moved Permanently) assigns a new permanent URI that future references should use, while 302 (Found) means the resource is temporarily elsewhere, so the client keeps using the original URI; 301 is heuristically cacheable.

For historical reasons a client may turn a POST into a GET after 301 or 302; 308 (Permanent Redirect) and 307 (Temporary Redirect) avoid this, and 307 forbids changing the method on automatic redirection.

303 (See Other) redirects to a different resource that gives an indirect response; it is mainly used to send the output of a POST to a resource that can be separately identified, bookmarked and cached.
304 (Not Modified) means a conditional GET or HEAD would have given 200 but its condition was false, so the client's stored representation is still valid and no content is sent.
A user agent may automatically follow the Location header even for an unknown 3xx code, but needs care with methods not known to be safe.

When following a redirect, the client replaces the target URI, drops automatically generated connection and origin-specific headers, and should consider removing headers such as Authorization and Cookie for security.
A client should detect and break cyclical redirection; an earlier specification advised at most five redirections, and some clients still enforce such a limit.

title: HTTP client error status codes

definition.text: The 4xx class says the client seems to have erred; the server should explain the error and whether it is temporary or permanent, and the codes apply to any method.

facts.text: 400 (Bad Request) means the server will not process the request because of a perceived client error, such as malformed syntax, invalid message framing or deceptive routing.

401 (Unauthorized) means the request lacks valid authentication credentials and must carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge, while 403 (Forbidden) means the server understood the request but refuses it, even with credentials that are insufficient.

404 (Not Found) means no current representation was found, or the server will not disclose one; it does not say whether this is permanent, and 410 (Gone) is preferred when the condition is likely permanent.
405 (Method Not Allowed) means the method is known but not supported by the target resource, and the response must list the supported methods in an Allow header.
409 (Conflict) means the request conflicts with the target resource's current state, and the user might be able to resolve it and resubmit.
412 (Precondition Failed) means a precondition in the request headers evaluated to false, preventing the method when the resource is in an unexpected state.

413 (Content Too Large), 414 (URI Too Long) and 415 (Unsupported Media Type) mean the request content is too big, its URI too long, or its format unsupported; a temporary 413 should carry Retry-After.
408 (Request Timeout) means the server did not receive a complete request in time, and the client may repeat the request, on a new connection if needed.

notes: more on the existing entry: adds 429, 428, 422 and 431, which the RFC 9110 sections used in round one do not cover (429 is RFC 6585).

definition.text: The 5xx class says the server is aware it has erred or cannot perform the requested method.

facts.text: 500 (Internal Server Error) means the server hit an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request.
501 (Not Implemented) means the server does not support the functionality needed, for example when it does not recognize the request method and cannot support it for any resource.

502 (Bad Gateway) means a server acting as a gateway or proxy received an invalid response from the inbound server, and 504 (Gateway Timeout) means it did not get a timely response from an upstream server.

503 (Service Unavailable) means the server cannot currently handle the request because of temporary overload or scheduled maintenance, and it may send Retry-After to say how long to wait; an overloaded server might simply refuse connections instead.
Retry-After holds either an HTTP-date or a number of seconds to wait; with 503 it says how long the service is expected to be unavailable.
505 (HTTP Version Not Supported) means the server does not support the major HTTP version in the request.

title: HTTP origins and certificate verification
article: rfc>9110#4. Identifiers in HTTP > 4.3. Authoritative Access > 4.3.4. https Certificate Verification

definition.text: An origin is the scheme, host and port of a URI, and for https URIs a client must verify that the server's certificate matches that origin before trusting the connection.

facts.text: The origin of a URI is the triple of scheme, host and port after normalization.

For http, authority belongs to whoever controls the server listening on the port; for https, it rests on the server's ability to use the private key matching a certificate the client trusts for that origin.

A client must verify that the service's identity matches the URI's origin server, to prevent impersonation by an on-path attacker or one controlling name resolution; this requires configured trust anchors.

If the certificate is not valid for the origin, the user agent must get user confirmation or end the connection with a bad certificate error, since ignoring the server's identity leaves the connection open to active attack.

title: Keeping sensitive data out of URLs
article: rfc>9110#17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs

definition.text: URIs are meant to be shared, not secured, so sensitive or personally identifiable information should not be placed in them.

facts.text: URIs appear on displays, in printed pages and unprotected bookmarks, and many servers, proxies and user agents log or display them where third parties can see them.

A GET form builds a URI from user input, so POST is often preferred for sensitive fields because it sends them in the content, but this hinders caching and uses an unsafe method for what would be a safe request.

Alternatives are to transform or filter the data before building the URI, or to redirect the query result to a server-generated URI, which removes sensitive data from later links and gives a cacheable response.
The Referer header can reveal a user's recent browsing history and any personal data in the referring URI.

definition.text: HTTP has generic extension points, such as methods, status codes, header fields, authentication schemes and cache directives, that add capabilities without a new protocol version.

facts.text: Because the semantics of HTTP are not versioned, these extension points persist and mean the same in every version.
Version-specific extension points, such as transfer codings in HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 frame types, cannot override a version-independent mechanism unless that element allows it, as CONNECT does.
New methods and status codes should be registered in the IANA HTTP Method and Status Code registries.

title: HTTP caching

definition.text: An HTTP cache is a local store of earlier responses, with the subsystem that controls their storage, retrieval and deletion, which reuses a prior response to answer a later request and so improves performance.

facts.text: A cache stores cacheable responses to reduce response time and network bandwidth on future equivalent requests, and a cached response shortens the request-response chain for any participant that holds one.

Caching is optional in HTTP, but reuse is the default when nothing prevents it, so the rules focus on stopping a cache from storing a non-reusable response or reusing a stored one inappropriately; correct operation preserves HTTP semantics.
The cache key is at least the request method and target URI; many caches store only GET responses and so key on the URI alone, while the Vary header adds request fields to the key.

Most commonly a cache stores a 200 (OK) response to a GET, but it may also store redirects, negative results such as 404, incomplete 206 results, and responses to other methods whose definition allows it.
Browsers cache resources they fetched, busy sites use web cache servers, and deployments include proxy cache hierarchies and content delivery networks with gateway caches.

A cache can use one stored or storable response for many requests, so it can collapse several incoming requests into a single forward request on a miss, reducing load on the origin server and network.
A cache must write unsafe requests through to the origin before replying, and such requests may invalidate stored responses.
A cache that cannot reach the origin is disconnected and can serve stale responses in some circumstances.

notes: One of the entries that the course's general Caching chapter may overlap; this one is the HTTP-specific standard (RFC 9111).

title: Storing and reusing HTTP cached responses

definition.text: A cache may store a response only if it passes storage checks and may reuse a stored response only if the new request matches it and the response is fresh, allowed stale or validated.

facts.text: A cache must not store a response unless it understands the request method, the status code is final, and the response has no no-store directive; a shared cache also needs no restricting private directive.
A cache may reuse a stored response only if the target URIs match, the stored method allows it, and the request headers nominated by Vary match.
Even then the response must not carry no-cache unless successfully validated, and it must be fresh, allowed to be served stale, or successfully validated.
A shared cache must not reuse a response to a request with an Authorization header unless a response directive (must-revalidate, public or s-maxage) allows it.

title: HTTP cache freshness
article: rfc>9111#4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness

definition.text: A cached response is fresh while its age has not exceeded its freshness lifetime, and a fresh response can be reused without contacting the origin server.

facts.text: Freshness lifetime is the time between the origin generating a response and its expiration time, and age is the time since the origin generated or last successfully validated it; a response is stale once age exceeds the lifetime.
The primary mechanism is an explicit expiration time from the origin, using the Expires header or the max-age directive; a time in the past forces validation on every request.
A cache takes the freshness lifetime from the first matching rule: s-maxage for a shared cache, then max-age, then the Expires value minus the Date value; otherwise no explicit expiration exists.

When no explicit expiration exists, a cache may assign a heuristic one, only for heuristically cacheable status codes or explicitly cacheable responses, and it should use no more than some fraction, typically 10%, of the interval since Last-Modified.
The Age header carries the cache's estimate of seconds since the origin generated or validated the response, summing the time in each cache on the path and the time in transit.
A cache computes current age as corrected initial age plus the time since it received the response.
The Expires header is ignored when the response has a max-age directive, and for a shared cache when it has s-maxage; invalid dates such as 0 mean already expired.
A cache must not serve a stale response if a directive forbids it, and otherwise only when disconnected or when the client or origin permits it, for example with max-stale.

title: HTTP cache validation
article: rfc>9111#4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.3. Validation

definition.text: Validation, or revalidation, is a cache using a conditional request to ask the next server whether a stored response is still valid instead of fetching it in full.

facts.text: A cache validates when it holds responses for a URI but cannot serve them, for example because they are stale; the forwarded request carries preconditions built from the stored response's validators.

The validators are the Last-Modified timestamp, sent in If-Modified-Since, and the ETag entity tags, sent in If-None-Match; a cache must send stored entity tags and should send the Last-Modified value as well.
A 304 (Not Modified) answer means the stored response can be updated and reused, so no content is transferred.
A full response means no stored response was suitable, so the cache uses it for the request and may store it.
If validation returns a 5xx, the cache may forward it, or act as if the server did not respond and send a stored response where allowed, or retry.
On a 304 the cache updates the stored responses it identifies by strong validator, or by weak validator, using the headers in the 304.
A cache can also send a HEAD request to update or invalidate stored GET responses when validators are missing or transferring content is not wanted.
Each client in a request chain may have its own cache, so an intermediary cache often receives conditional requests from other caches; If-None-Match takes precedence over If-Modified-Since.

title: HTTP cache invalidation
article: rfc>9111#4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.4. Invalidating Stored Responses

definition.text: Invalidation is a cache removing or marking invalid its stored responses for a URI, so a mandatory validation is needed before any is used again.

facts.text: Unsafe methods such as PUT, POST or DELETE can change state on the origin, so intervening caches are required to invalidate stored responses to keep their contents current.
A cache must invalidate the target URI when it receives a non-error response, with a 2xx or 3xx status, to an unsafe method, including methods whose safety is unknown.
A cache may also invalidate other URIs, such as those in Location and Content-Location, but never when their origin differs from the target URI's, which prevents denial-of-service attacks.
Invalidation is not global: a state-changing request invalidates responses only in the caches it travels through.

definition.text: The Cache-Control header lists directives that control caches along the request and response chain.

facts.text: Cache directives are unidirectional: a directive in a request does not imply the same directive in the response.
A proxy, whether or not it implements a cache, must pass cache directives through in forwarded messages, and it is not possible to target a directive at a specific cache.
Request directives are advisory, which caches may implement but need not, while a cache must obey the response directives.
Cache-Control takes precedence over the older Expires header, which is ignored when max-age or, for a shared cache, s-maxage is present.

title: Cache-Control response directives
article: rfc>9111#5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.2. Response Directives

definition.text: Response directives are instructions from the origin server that tell caches whether and for how long a response may be stored and reused.

facts.text: max-age says the response is stale once its age exceeds the given seconds, and s-maxage overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches and also requires them to revalidate once stale.
no-cache means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation, while no-store means a cache must not store any part of the request or response.
no-store is not a reliable or sufficient privacy mechanism, since compromised caches may ignore it and networks may be eavesdropped.
private means a shared cache must not store the response because it is for a single user, though a private cache may; it controls where a response can be stored, not the privacy of its content.
public explicitly marks a response as cacheable, even for a request with an Authorization header, though it is unnecessary on a response that is already cacheable.
must-revalidate means that once stale a response must not be reused until the origin validates it, even when the cache is disconnected, in which case a cache should return 504 (Gateway Timeout).
Servers should use must-revalidate only when failing to validate could cause incorrect operation, such as a silently unexecuted financial transaction.
proxy-revalidate is like must-revalidate but applies only to shared caches, and no-transform forbids intermediaries from transforming the content.

title: Cache-Control request directives
article: rfc>9111#5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives

definition.text: Request directives let a client suggest how a cache should treat a request, but they are advisory and caches need not honor them.

facts.text: max-age asks for a response no older than the given seconds, max-stale accepts a response past its freshness lifetime, optionally by a limit, and min-fresh wants one that stays fresh for at least the given seconds.
no-cache asks that a stored response not be used without successful validation at the origin, and no-store says a cache must not store any part of the request or its response.
only-if-cached asks for a stored response only, and a cache that honors it answers with one or with 504 (Gateway Timeout).

definition.text: A shared cache stores responses for reuse by more than one user and sits usually in an intermediary, while a private cache is dedicated to one user, often inside a user agent.

facts.text: The private response directive stops a shared cache from storing a response meant for one user, but a private cache may store it.
A shared cache needs extra permission to reuse a response to an Authorization request, and s-maxage applies only to shared caches.
Private caches are limited to one user, so they can be used to reconstruct that user's activity and users should be able to remove stored responses.

definition.text: Caches add an attack surface, because their contents persist after a request ends and an attack on a cache can reveal or alter information long afterwards.

facts.text: In cache poisoning an attacker inserts a malicious response into a cache, which is especially effective when a shared cache distributes it to many clients; one vector is differences in message parsing between proxies and user agents.
Cache timing leaks which resources were previously requested, since a fast load shows a site was visited; adding the referring site to the cache key, called double keying, mitigates it.
Deployment flaws can cache sensitive information, such as authentication credentials, and a cacheable response with Set-Cookie can be reused for later requests.

definition.text: An HTTP cookie is a small block of data that a web server creates and the user's browser stores and sends back, giving stateless HTTP a memory of earlier requests.

facts.text: A server sets a cookie with a Set-Cookie response header; the browser stores it and sends it back with every request, introducing state into otherwise stateless HTTP transactions.
A cookie is a name and value plus attributes such as expiry, domain and flags; browsers do not send attributes to the server but use them to decide when to delete, block or send the cookie.
A session cookie has no Expires or Max-Age and is deleted when the browser closes; a persistent cookie expires at a set date or after a set time and is often used to keep users logged in.
Expires sets the deletion date, Max-Age sets seconds from receipt, and a server removes a cookie by sending an expiration date in the past; Domain and Path define its scope.
A cookie can only be set for the current resource's top domain and its subdomains; without a Domain attribute it is host-only and is not sent to subdomains.
A session cookie usually holds only a unique session identifier while the server keeps the cart or user data in a database, so cookie size does not limit it and the cookie uses little bandwidth.
Authentication cookies show the server a user is logged in: after a successful login the server remembers that the session identifier is authenticated, so users need not log in on every page.
A third-party cookie belongs to a domain other than the one in the address bar, such as an ad server, and lets advertisers build a browsing history of a user across every site carrying their content.

title: Securing cookies
article: HTTP cookie#Cookie theft and session hijacking

definition.text: Securing cookies means protecting the session identifiers that cookies carry from theft and misuse, using encryption, cookie attributes and input filtering.

facts.text: Most sites use cookies as the only identifier of a user session, so an attacker who steals a victim's full set of cookies is treated by the server as the victim's session.

Cookies sent over unencrypted HTTP can be read by anyone on the network, such as on open Wi-Fi; TLS fixes this, and the Secure attribute makes the browser send the cookie only over an encrypted channel.
A Secure cookie set from a non-secure connection can still be intercepted by a man-in-the-middle attack, so Secure cookies should only be set over a secure connection.

Cross-site scripting steals cookies by getting attacker JavaScript to send document.cookie to the attacker; an HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by client-side scripts, which mitigates this, though developers must still filter malicious code.

Cross-site request forgery abuses automatic cookie sending: browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request to it, so a forged request from another page looks real to a server that trusts the cookie.

SameSite=Strict sends cookies only when the target domain matches the origin, which mitigates CSRF; Lax also allows safe requests such as GET; None allows cross-site cookies, and most browsers require Secure with it.

definition.text: HTTP pipelining is a feature of HTTP/1.1 that lets a client send several HTTP requests over one TCP connection without waiting for the matching responses.

facts.text: Pipelining dramatically improves page load times, especially on high-latency links such as satellite connections, but the server must answer in the order requests arrived, so the connection stays first-in-first-out and head-of-line blocking can occur.

GET and HEAD requests can always be pipelined, non-idempotent requests such as POST should not be, and other idempotent requests like PUT and DELETE can be pipelined if they do not depend on each other's effects.
Many legacy servers and especially proxies handle pipelining badly, even mixing up the order of responses, so most clients do not use it and browsers disabled or removed it.
HTTP/2 multiplexing superseded pipelining, and in HTTP/3 multiplexing is done by QUIC, which also avoids head-of-line blocking when packets are lost.

definition.text: A 1xx status code is an interim response that reports connection status or request progress before the final response.

facts.text: A 1xx response ends with the header section and has no content; a server MUST NOT send one to an HTTP/1.0 client, and a client MUST be able to parse one or more before a final response.

100 (Continue) says the initial part of a request was received and not rejected; a client sends Expect: 100-continue and waits for it before a large body, so a request rejected on its headers wastes no upload.

101 (Switching Protocols) answers a client's Upgrade request: the server MUST send an Upgrade header naming the protocol now in effect, as in the WebSocket handshake or a switch to a newer HTTP version.
103 (Early Hints) returns some response headers before the final message; 102 (Processing), a WebDAV code that kept clients from timing out on long requests, is deprecated.

title: Non-standard HTTP status codes
article: List of HTTP status codes#Nonstandard codes

definition.text: Non-standard status codes are values that web servers, proxies and platforms use although no IETF standard defines them.

facts.text: IETF-defined codes are documented in RFCs and maintained by IANA, while other values are used by various servers; the reason phrase after a code can differ from the typical one or be omitted.

nginx expands the 4xx space: 444 closes the connection with no response, 495 and 496 report an invalid or missing client certificate, 497 an HTTP request to an HTTPS port, and 499 a client that closed the request early.

Cloudflare's reverse proxy expands 5xx to signal origin problems: 521 the origin refused connections, 522 contact timed out, 524 TCP connected but no timely HTTP response, 525 and 526 TLS handshake or certificate failures.
Some HTTP proxies informally use 598 to signal a network read timeout and 599 a network connect timeout behind the proxy to a client in front of it.

definition.text: Public-key cryptography, or asymmetric cryptography, uses pairs of related keys, a public key that can be shared openly and a private key that must stay secret.

facts.text: Key pairs are generated with algorithms based on one-way functions, and security depends on keeping the private key secret; the public key can be distributed openly without compromising security.

It removes the key-distribution burden of symmetric ciphers, where both sides need the same secret key exchanged securely first and each pair of users needs a separate key; only private keys need protecting.
In public-key encryption anyone with the public key can encrypt but only the private-key holder can decrypt; this hides the message content but does not tell the recipient who sent it.

In a digital signature the sender signs a message with the private key and anyone with the public key can verify it; a forger without the private key cannot make a valid signature, so software updates can be shown genuine.

Public-key algorithms are far more computationally intensive than symmetric ones, so TLS, SSH and PGP are hybrid: a public-key exchange shares a symmetric key, which then encrypts the data at higher throughput without pre-sharing a key.
The key problem is proving a public key is authentic: if an attacker swaps in their own public key, a man-in-the-middle attack lets them intercept, decrypt and re-encrypt messages for each segment.

A public key infrastructure of certificate authorities certifies key ownership, and TLS relies on it; a web of trust, as in PGP, uses individual endorsements instead; subverting a trusted authority still enables man-in-the-middle attacks.

The chief risk is that a private key becomes known, which recent TLS mitigates with forward secrecy and ephemeral keys; quantum computing makes many asymmetric algorithms vulnerable, so quantum-resistant schemes are being developed.

title: Diffie-Hellman key exchange

definition.text: Diffie-Hellman key exchange is a mathematical method of securely generating a shared symmetric key over a public channel.

facts.text: It lets two parties with no prior knowledge of each other jointly establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel, replacing key exchange by courier; the key then encrypts later traffic with a symmetric cipher.

Both parties publicly agree on a prime modulus p and base g, each picks a secret number and sends g raised to it mod p, then raises the received value to its own secret to reach the same shared value.

Only the two secret numbers stay private; p, g and both exchanged values travel in the clear, and an eavesdropper must solve the discrete logarithm problem, which is hard for large groups; primes of at least 2048 bits are recommended.

Diffie-Hellman by itself is a non-authenticated key-agreement protocol, so authentication must be added, for example with a pre-shared public key or a shared password, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

Ephemeral keys give forward secrecy: new key pairs are generated for each session and discarded afterwards, which is practical because Diffie-Hellman key generation is cheap; TLS uses this in its ephemeral modes.

Much Internet traffic uses a handful of groups of 1024 bits or less, so an attacker can precompute the costly first steps of the number field sieve once; the Logjam attack exploited export-grade 512-bit groups.

Ephemeral variants are open to denial of service because an attacker can send arbitrary numbers that are not public keys, forcing the victim into expensive modular exponentiation (the D(HE)at attack).

Quantum computers using Shor's algorithm can break RSA, finite-field Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, so a 2023 post-quantum variant combines CRYSTALS-Kyber with the X25519 elliptic curve.
