definition.text: A chain of trust lets a certificate be validated against its parent certificates, back to a root certificate that serves as a trust anchor.

facts.text: A public-key certificate ties a public key to its subject and carries the issuer's digital signature; a client that trusts the issuer and finds a valid signature can use the key to interact securely with the subject.

A root certificate is the self-signed trust anchor with no parent; intermediate certificates only sign other certificates and must themselves be signed by a root or another intermediate; a leaf certificate cannot sign others.

In certification path validation of a server certificate, the client checks that the certificate's subject matches the hostname it connects to and that a trusted certificate authority signed it, then sets up the encrypted connection.

Browsers and operating systems ship lists of default-trusted certificate authorities set by root programs; Firefox uses the Mozilla program everywhere, while Chrome, Edge and Safari mostly use the operating system's trust store.
Root programs record the valid purposes of each root with trust bits, so a CA can be trusted for TLS server certificates but not for code signing.

A certificate is requested from a CA with a signing request sent through an enrollment protocol such as CMP, EST or ACME, and the issuer bears the main responsibility for verifying its authenticity, integrity and authorization.

A self-signed certificate has a subject matching its issuer and is worthless for trust between unacquainted parties, but fully trusted when the issuer and sole user are the same; public Internet servers need certificates from a trusted public CA.

definition.text: TLS certificates come in several types by what they identify: servers, clients, several names at once, or whole families of subdomains.

facts.text: A server certificate proves the server is the intended destination; a client certificate authenticates the client for access control, usually names a person, and is issued by the service provider, though username and password is more common.

A Subject Alternative Name (SAN) certificate lists several values, such as DNS names and IP addresses, in its subjectAltName field; SANs are the preferred place for DNS names, and Chrome 58 stopped checking commonName at all.

A wildcard certificate uses an asterisk so one certificate secures many subdomains, but only one level: *.example.com matches sub1.example.com, not example.com or deeper names; an Extended Validation certificate cannot be a wildcard.

Other certificates include S/MIME email certificates, code-signing certificates that show binaries were not tampered with, qualified certificates identifying an individual for electronic signatures, and EMV payment-card issuer certificates.

title: Certificate validation levels
article: Public key certificate#Website security > Validation levels

definition.text: Validation levels describe how much a certificate authority checks before issuing a certificate: domain control only, organization identity, or extended legal identity.

facts.text: A domain-validated (DV) certificate is issued when the purchaser shows the right to administratively manage the DNS domain; its techniques prove control of a domain name, not information about the applicant's identity.

An organization-validated (OV) certificate also needs the organization's actual existence as a legal entity, and an Extended Validation (EV) certificate needs manual human checks of legal identity; providers publish their criteria in a certificate policy.

Domain validation is always vulnerable to attacks that let an adversary observe the CA's validation probes, such as attacks on DNS, TCP or BGP; a common method emails a token to an administrative address like admin@ or postmaster@.
EV does not fully fix this because an attacker could still get a domain-validated certificate for the victim domain; until 2019 major browsers showed the legal identity for EV certificates.

title: Certificate authority trust risks

definition.text: A certificate authority is a trusted third party that stores, signs and issues digital certificates, so the whole system's security depends on it.

facts.text: A CA verifies an applicant's credentials before certifying that a public key belongs to the named entity; it is trusted by both the certificate's owner and the relying party, and client software ships with a set of trusted CA certificates.
X.509's critical weakness is that any CA a party trusts can issue a certificate for any domain; with dozens of trusted CAs in a browser, subverting one lets an attacker impersonate any site.

An attacker who steals a CA's private keys can forge certificates without further access, so publicly trusted CAs keep keys in hardware security modules and the long-term root key in an offline one, signing only shorter-lived intermediates.

The CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements, needed for inclusion in the Firefox and Safari stores, cap certificate lifetime: 60 months from 1st July 2012, 398 Days from 1 September 2020, and 47 Days from 15 March 2029.

Certificate Transparency requires all TLS certificates to be logged in publicly auditable records to detect fraudulent ones in real time, and has largely superseded HTTP Public Key Pinning, which browsers deprecated for its risk of bricking sites.

Commercial CAs charge for certificates and want their root in most browsers, a reach called ubiquity; non-profits such as Let's Encrypt and some cloud providers also issue publicly trusted certificates.

definition.text: A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack, or on-path attack, is one where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are talking directly.

facts.text: In active eavesdropping the attacker makes independent connections with both victims and relays messages, controlling the whole conversation; this needs intercepting all relevant messages and injecting new ones, which is easy near an unencrypted Wi-Fi access point.
The attack succeeds only if the attacker impersonates each endpoint well enough to satisfy it, since it aims to circumvent mutual authentication.

Mallory replaces Bob's public key with her own, so Alice encrypts to Mallory, who decrypts, reads or alters the message and re-encrypts it with Bob's key; the parties need a way to know they hold real keys.

Variants include HTTPS spoofing with a fake certificate, SSL/TLS stripping that downgrades HTTPS to HTTP, ARP spoofing, DNS spoofing, session hijacking, evil-twin Wi-Fi and certificates signed by a fraudulent CA.

Defenses are authentication and tamper detection; most cryptographic protocols authenticate endpoints, for example TLS authenticating one or both parties through a mutually trusted certificate authority, and DNSSEC signs DNS records against redirects to malicious IPs.
Mutual authentication, where server and client validate each other, covers both ends, but most connections authenticate only the server, so MITM attacks can still occur.
Tamper detection can notice an attack through abnormal response times, because an interceptor adds latency to a transaction.

The attacker does not break the encryption: after decrypting a message, the snoop re-encrypts it with a key shared with the real recipient, or their public key in asymmetric systems, and sends it on to avoid detection.

definition.text: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) lets a website tell browsers to use only HTTPS connections to it, protecting against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrades and cookie hijacking.

facts.text: A server sets the policy with the Strict-Transport-Security response header, which is honored only over an HTTPS connection; max-age is in seconds, so max-age=31536000 keeps the policy for one non-leap year.

While a policy is in effect the browser rewrites insecure links to https before contacting the server, and must end the connection, without letting the user continue, if it cannot be secured, such as when the certificate is untrusted.
HSTS fixes SSL stripping, where an attacker silently turns an HTTPS connection into plain HTTP with no warning; without it the user cannot know whether the connection should have been secure.

Protection relies on trust on first use: the first visit, and the first request after max-age expires, are unprotected, and an attacker can strip the header on a first visit; sites should set a period of days or months.
Browsers ship a preload list of known HSTS sites so that even the first request uses HTTPS; domains can be added at no cost, but such a list cannot scale to cover every website.
Best practice is for an HSTS host to answer with the header at its top-level domain too, with the includeSubDomains directive, which helps avoid threats such as cookie injection attacks.

HSTS cannot stop attacks on TLS itself or on a compromised server, is ineffective against look-alike or spoofed domains, and, being time limited, can be defeated by shifting the victim's clock with false NTP packets.
Because browsers must persistently cache the policy and RFC 6797 makes deleting it deliberately hard, HSTS state can tag a visiting browser with identifying data that survives clearing cookies.

definition.text: Symmetric-key encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt plaintext and to decrypt ciphertext, so both parties must hold that shared secret.

facts.text: The keys are in practice a shared secret between the parties, and the need for both to have the secret key is the main drawback compared with asymmetric (public-key) encryption.
Symmetric algorithms are usually better for bulk encryption: apart from the one-time pad they have smaller keys, which means less storage space and faster transmission.

Modern systems use Diffie-Hellman or another public-key protocol to agree on a fresh secret key for each session, then encrypt the bulk of the messages symmetrically, so no physically secure channel is needed.
Symmetric encryption uses either stream ciphers, which encrypt a message one digit or byte at a time, or block ciphers, which encrypt a block of bits as one unit; AES uses 128-bit blocks.
Popular algorithms include AES (Rijndael), ChaCha20, Salsa20, Twofish, Camellia and Blowfish.
Encrypting a message does not guarantee it stays unchanged, so a message authentication code is often added to the ciphertext; one can be built from an AEAD cipher such as AES-GCM.
Grover's algorithm would cut a brute-force attack to the square root of the time, which doubling the key length compensates for; AES-256 is therefore believed to be quantum resistant.
Session keys come from pseudorandom key generators, and weak randomness in them or in initialization vectors has led to cryptanalytic breaks, so implementations need a high-entropy source.

definition.text: An HTTP/2 stream is an independent, bidirectional sequence of frames within one connection, and giving each request and response its own stream is how HTTP/2 multiplexes requests.

facts.text: One HTTP/2 connection can hold many concurrently open streams, with either endpoint interleaving frames from different streams; each request and response exchange is associated with its own stream.
Streams are largely independent, so a blocked or stalled request or response does not stop progress on other streams, although TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed by HTTP/2.

The basic unit is the frame, with a fixed 9-octet header; payloads over 2^14 (16,384) octets are not sent unless the receiver set a larger SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE, and HEADERS and DATA frames carry requests and responses.
Stream identifiers are 31-bit integers; clients use odd numbers and servers even, each new identifier must exceed all earlier ones from that endpoint, and identifiers are never reused.
A long-lived connection can run out of identifiers; a client then opens a new connection and a server sends a GOAWAY frame to force the client to open one.
A stream goes through idle, open, reserved, half-closed and closed states: END_STREAM half-closes it, and it is closed once both sides have sent END_STREAM or either side sends RST_STREAM.

SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS limits the streams a peer may open, in one direction; it is initially unlimited, and a value no smaller than 100 is recommended so parallelism is not needlessly limited.

A connection error prevents further processing, so the endpoint sends GOAWAY and closes the TCP connection, while a stream error sends RST_STREAM for that stream only and does not affect other streams.

title: HTTP/2 flow control
article: rfc>9113#5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control

definition.text: HTTP/2 flow control is a credit-based scheme, driven by the receiver, that keeps multiplexed streams on one connection from destructively interfering with each other.

facts.text: Using streams for multiplexing creates contention over the TCP connection and can block streams; flow control applies to individual streams and to the connection as a whole, through WINDOW_UPDATE frames.

Receivers advertise how many octets they will accept; the initial window is 65,535 octets for each new stream and for the connection, and only DATA frames count against it, so control frames are never blocked.

Flow control works hop by hop, not end to end, and protects resource-constrained endpoints such as a proxy with a slow upstream and fast downstream; advertising the maximum window of 2^31-1 effectively disables it.

If a peer's window is smaller than the bandwidth * delay product, receive throughput is limited and performance degrades; timely WINDOW_UPDATE frames help, and endpoints must read frames promptly to avoid deadlock.

title: HTTP/2 header compression
article: rfc>9113#4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression

definition.text: HTTP/2 compresses each set of header fields into a field block (HPACK) using state shared across the connection, which shrinks the repetitive headers HTTP carries.

facts.text: HTTP fields are often repetitive and verbose, causing unnecessary traffic and quickly filling the initial TCP congestion window; compressing them lets many requests fit into one packet.
Compression is stateful: each endpoint keeps an HPACK encoder and decoder context with a dynamic table, whose maximum size the decoder sets with SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE, starting at 4,096 bytes.

Field blocks must travel as a contiguous run of HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE and CONTINUATION frames, and a receiver must decompress them even when discarding the frames, because they change compression state; a decoding error is a connection error.
The Cookie header may be split into separate fields, each with one or more cookie pairs, because updating one pair would otherwise invalidate the stored field line and hurt compression efficiency.

title: HTTP/2 server push
article: rfc>9113#8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push

definition.text: HTTP/2 server push lets a server send responses, with the promised requests that go with them, to a client before the client asks for them.

facts.text: The server synthesizes a request, sends it as a PUSH_PROMISE frame in association with an earlier client request, and then answers it on a separate server-initiated stream.

Push aims to remove a round trip: a request for HTML is often followed by requests for the stylesheets and scripts it references, and pushing them spares the client from waiting to read those references.

In practice push is hard to use well, because the server must predict requests despite caching, content negotiation and user behavior; wrong guesses waste bandwidth and large pushes can contend with more important responses.

Promised requests must be safe and cacheable and carry no content; a client can turn push off per hop by setting SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH to 0, and a client resets a promised stream that breaks these rules.

definition.text: An HTTP/2 connection starts with TLS and the ALPN extension for https URIs, or with prior knowledge for cleartext http, and each side then sends a connection preface.

facts.text: An http or https URI does not say which HTTP versions the server supports; for https the client uses TLS with the ALPN extension and the identifier h2, and both sides MUST then send a connection preface.

Support over cleartext http can only be known out of band; a client with that prior knowledge opens a TCP connection and sends the preface, and the h2c Upgrade mechanism was never widely deployed and is deprecated.

The client preface is the 24-octet string PRI * HTTP/2.0 followed by SETTINGS, the server's first frame is a SETTINGS frame, and clients may send more frames at once without waiting for the server's preface.
HTTP/2 over TLS MUST use TLS 1.2 or higher with the SNI extension, and over TLS 1.2 deployments MUST disable TLS compression and renegotiation.

definition.text: HTTP/2 uses one long-lived, persistent connection per host and port, reused across requests and shut down gracefully with a GOAWAY frame.

facts.text: Clients keep connections open until no more communication is needed and SHOULD NOT open more than one per host and port, except to replace one near exhausting stream identifiers, needing fresh TLS keys or failed.

A connection may serve several origins while the server is authoritative, which for https requires a certificate valid for the host; a server that does not want reuse answers 421 (Misdirected Request).

Before closing, an endpoint should send GOAWAY naming the highest stream that might have been processed; requests on higher streams, or on a stream reset with REFUSED_STREAM, were unprocessed and are safe to retry.
Idle connections can silently break because middleboxes such as NATs or load balancers discard connection bindings, so a client can send a PING frame to test a connection without sending a request.

title: TLS 1.3

definition.text: TLS 1.3 is the current version of Transport Layer Security, designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery between client and server applications.

facts.text: TLS gives a secure channel over any reliable, in-order stream: the server is always authenticated and the client optionally, data is visible only to the endpoints, and tampering is detected even if an attacker controls the network.

TLS has two components: a handshake protocol that authenticates the parties, negotiates parameters and establishes keys, and is designed to resist tampering, and a record protocol that protects traffic in independently protected records.

TLS 1.3 pruned legacy features: only AEAD ciphers remain, static RSA and Diffie-Hellman suites are gone so all public-key key exchange gives forward secrecy, and compression and custom DHE groups were removed.
The handshake has three phases, key exchange, server parameters and authentication, and every handshake message after the ServerHello is now encrypted.

The ClientHello carries a random nonce, offered versions, cipher and hash pairs, and Diffie-Hellman key shares, PSK labels or both; the server's ServerHello selects the parameters, and the two messages together determine the shared keys.

Authentication uses a Certificate, a CertificateVerify that signs the entire handshake with the certificate's private key, and a Finished MAC over the handshake that confirms the keys; the client sends them too when asked.

If the client's key_share is unacceptable, the server sends a HelloRetryRequest and the client restarts with a suitable one; if no common parameters can be negotiated, the server MUST abort the handshake.

TLS supports three basic key exchange modes, including (EC)DHE and PSK with (EC)DHE, and key derivation was redesigned around HKDF, which cryptographers can analyze more easily thanks to better key separation.

definition.text: TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT) lets a client that shares a pre-shared key with the server send application data in its first flight, saving a round trip at the cost of weaker security.

facts.text: When both sides share a PSK, from an earlier handshake or out of band, the client encrypts early data under it in the first flight, added to the 1-RTT PSK handshake whose other messages are unchanged.
0-RTT data is weaker than other TLS data: it is not forward secret, being encrypted only under keys derived from the PSK, and nothing guarantees it is not replayed between connections.
Within one connection 0-RTT data cannot be duplicated, and an attacker cannot make it look like 1-RTT data because different keys protect it.

There are two threats: a network attacker duplicating a flight of 0-RTT data, and one exploiting client retries; the second cannot be prevented in TLS, and any application whose clients retry already needs its own anti-replay defense.

Clients cannot know what protection a server has, so they MUST send as early data only what is safe to replay; servers SHOULD ensure 0-RTT data is accepted at most once, by sharing state or equivalent means.

Single-use tickets allow each ticket once, for example by deleting it from a ticket database on use and doing a full handshake for unknown tickets; sharing that database across distributed servers makes high 0-RTT success rates hard.

ClientHello recording stores a unique value from each ClientHello within a time window and rejects duplicates; it is easier to distribute but weaker, and with several zones the best defense makes one zone authoritative per ticket.

Freshness checks accept 0-RTT only for a ClientHello that arrives about when expected, from the ticket's creation time plus an estimated round-trip time and the client's ticket age; otherwise the server falls back to 1-RTT.

definition.text: RFC 6585 defines four optional HTTP status codes, 428, 429, 431 and 511, for common situations that less precise codes handled poorly.

facts.text: These codes are optional and servers cannot be required to support them; clients treat an unknown code as the generic code of its class, so existing servers can deploy them safely, and responses using them MUST NOT be cached.

428 Precondition Required says the server requires a conditional request, typically to avoid the lost update problem, where a client GETs a resource, modifies it and PUTs it back while a third party changed it.
429 Too Many Requests says the user sent too many requests in a given time; the response may include a Retry-After header, and the RFC leaves open how the server identifies users and counts requests.

431 means the request headers, in total or one field, are too large and the request may be resubmitted after shrinking them; 511 means the client must authenticate for network access and comes from intercepting proxies, not origin servers.

title: RSA cryptosystem

definition.text: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem in which publicly revealing the encryption key does not reveal the decryption key, so anyone can encrypt for the key's owner and the owner can sign messages.

facts.text: Revealing the encryption key publicly does not reveal the decryption key, so no couriers or other secure means are needed to transmit keys.
A message is enciphered with the key its intended recipient has publicly revealed, and only that recipient, who knows the corresponding decryption key, can decipher it.

A message can be signed with a privately held decryption key and anyone can verify the signature with the public encryption key; signatures cannot be forged, and a signer cannot later deny a valid signature.
Encryption represents the message as a number M, raises it to a publicly specified power e, and takes the remainder when divided by n, the public product of two large secret primes p and q.
Decryption is similar but uses a secret power d, where e * d is congruent to 1 modulo (p - 1) * (q - 1); security rests in part on the difficulty of factoring the published n.
In practice public-key encryption is often used to exchange the secret key for symmetric encryption, which is better for bulk data.
